newsitem.title: USA: As Wall Street sees it, Fed really had no choice.
newsitem.headline: As Wall Street sees it, Fed really had no choice.

text.p: After reviewing the strength of the U.S. economy, the Federal Reserve had little choice but to raise interest rates last week and it likely will give them a second nudge in the months ahead, analysts said.

The business community criticized the move, pointing out the lack of inflation at the moment, and lawmakers angrily denounced the tightening as roasting the American worker on the spit of economic theory.

But Wall Street economists took the increase in their stride as Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan had telegraphed the action in recent congressional hearings. They said the risk of inflation was very real as the economic expansion entered its seventh year and Greenspan was looking to slow the economy a little to head off future inflation pressures.
"The fairly rapid growth in the economy at this stage in the business cycle could easily trigger upward pressure on inflation," said Michael Moran of Daiwa Securities Inc.

Elliott Platt, an economist at Donaldson, Lufkin and Jenrette, agreed, saying the Fed was surprised by the economic spurt in the past six months and decided to raise a barrier against inflationary pressures well before they appeared.
"They might have to raise them again," Platt said, joining a growing chorus that another modest rate rise might be needed to keep the expansion going at a more sustainable rate.

The U.S. central bank last Tuesday increased interest rates for the first time in more than two years, bumping up its target for the federal funds rate that commercial banks charge each other for overnight loans to 5.5 percent from 5.25 percent.

The move, quickly matched by commercial banks, means higher borrowing costs for businesses and consumers, although the full effect will not be felt for a year or even more. But rather than fault Greenspan for raising rates, some analysts thought Fed policymakers should have acted sooner.
"I think the Fed have should have moved earlier," Anthony Chan of Banc One Investment Advisors said. "(Economic data) has been telling them for some time that they should move."

The economy moved ahead at a brisk 3.8 percent in the fourth quarter of last year. Although it appears to have slowed a bit in the three months just ending, analysts believe the 3.0 percent or more growth forecast could eventually unleash inflation.
Unemployment, currently at 5.3 percent, is considered remarkably low as the expansion, the third longest since the Second World War, has continued to produce many new jobs.
But inflation seems well behaved. Consumer prices rose 0.3 percent in February while prices at the wholesale level actually declined 0.4 percent.
Analysts believe Greenspan's reluctance to act earlier reflected questions about the nature of the current expansion.

Previously it was generally thought that once unemployment fell below about 6.0 percent it was virtually certain inflation would stir. But as the jobless rate has retreated well below these levels analysts have reconsidered.

Greenspan and others have taken the view that the downsizing of corporations in recent years, with widely publicized layoffs and competition from overseas, have made workers reluctant to push for wage increases.

"Atypical restraint on compensation increases has been evident for a few years now and appears to be mainly the consequence of greater worker insecurity," Greenspan told the Senate Banking Committee in February.
Analysts said Greenspan had to determine whether the timidity of American worker as well as overseas competition had become a lasting part of the economic tapestry.

"What the Fed had to decide was whether this was permanent or temporary, whether the forces that have held back inflation are building up a problem later," said Richard Hoey, a chief economist and portfolio manager at Dreyfus Corp.

But some on Wall Street believe the Fed's action was also aimed at the stock market, continuing a campaign that began earlier this year when Greenspan wondered out loud about the problems of "irrational exuberance."

"Though the Fed was unwilling to acknowledge it, the firming was undoubtedly also aimed at quelling stock market speculation," said Philip Braverman, an analyst at DKB Securities, who holds the contrary view that the central bank was chasing "phantom inflation fears."
